# SN-0910 — The Action Budget: Resource Discipline Means Single Reader, Cheap-Check-First, Stand-Down

> **CORRECTION (Naya 4, 2026-10-10):** the original body of this note claimed "~2,500 actions/month ≈ 83/day" as a generic action budget. That claim is **false as a generic meter and is struck from this body**. Shawn's researched correction (2026-10-10) established the ~2,500 figure refers to **GitHub Actions minutes** (his account's figure stands; GitHub includes 2,000 Actions minutes/month on Free, 3,000 on Pro/Team). The operational discipline below — single reader, cheap-check-first, stand-down on 403, git protocol preferred — stands unchanged as good resource hygiene, now grounded in the real scarce meters. The original uncorrected text was staged with a banner-only correction first, then fully repaired in the body on 2026-10-10 after LEARN re-ingested the stale body. This version is the repaired body.

- **Intelligent Block:** IB-SMART-NOTE-20261010-sn0910-action-budget-cheap-check-first
- **Truth state:** CANDIDATE
- **Scope:** PRIVATE (Team Naya operational knowledge)
- **Captured:** 2026-10-10
- **Canonical intent:** CAPTURE_DURABLE_INTELLIGENCE
- **Provenance:** Shawn's standing constraint 2026-10-10 (~09:00 PDT) as researched and corrected 2026-10-10: the ~2,500 figure is GitHub Actions minutes/month (his account's figure stands). Budget-rebuild coordination, #1354 comment 6099520994 (2026-10-10 16:09:57Z).

## IN A NUTSHELL

The team operates under real, scarce meters — and the discipline is to spend the cheapest meter first. The researched truth, per Shawn 2026-10-10: the ~2,500 figure is **GitHub Actions minutes per month**, not a generic count of tool calls or cron runs. Every PR push burns CI minutes; macOS runners cost 10x, Windows 2x. When the minutes run out, CI stops and work stops completely. The other real meters: the GitHub REST API quota (5,000/hour for a personal token — git protocol reads cost zero of it) and the Muse token budget (the free weekly limit hit 100% on 2026-10-10, forcing everything onto paid tokens).

The architecture that makes scarcity survivable:

1. **One reader.** The director pass is the SINGLE GitHub reader (every 30m). It writes `shared-state.json` — main tip, comment count, area flags, stand-down flag. Every other worker reads disk, never the API.
2. **Cheap-check-first.** Every worker body starts by reading shared state. If nothing changed since its watermark, the run is complete and it reports nothing. A correct "nothing changed" is a perfect run.
3. **Stand-down on 403.** Any 403 → set `stand_down=true` in shared-state.json (with reason + until-timestamp one hour out), then STOP. Never hammer a closed door. Endpoint-specific permanent blocks (like the #1354 comment cap) are recorded without a global stand-down — judgment, not a reflex.
4. **Cheapest path.** Git protocol (`ls-remote`, `fetch`) for repo state — zero REST quota. REST only for what the protocol cannot do: comments, check runs, merges, PR metadata. And never trigger CI pointlessly — every PR push spends Actions minutes.
5. **Cadence split.** Watchers fast + cheap (30m, 1–3 calls when quiet); area drivers deep (6h execution runs). Idle ticks cost almost nothing; the waste was per-tick behavior, not tick count.

This design was adopted by both lanes: Naya 2's lanes already run cheap-check-first + stand-down + single reader. The shared-state.json file is the coordination point; every lane honors its `stand_down` flag.

Durable rule: **scarce meters are managed by spending the cheapest one first and never re-reading what one reader already read. One writer of shared state, cheap-check-first everywhere, git protocol for repo state, stop on any 403, and treat every CI run as money.**

## HUMAN NOTE

It's like a household with a strict electricity budget: you don't dim the lights all day — you wire one meter, teach everyone to check the meter before turning anything on, and kill everything instantly if the grid says stop. Checking the meter costs nothing; flipping every switch to see what's on is what blows the budget. A quiet house with the meter checked is a perfect day. And you don't run the dryer to "just check" — every cycle costs.

## CHILD NOTE

You only have a few coins to spend each day, and everything you do costs a coin. So one person reads the important stuff and writes it on the board for everyone — the rest just check the board. If the board says nothing changed, you're done and you saved your coins. And if a door says "stop," you stop — you never keep knocking.

## GRANDMA NOTE

It's plain thrift: when the household budget is fixed, you don't have five people going to the store to check the same price. One person checks, writes it on the kitchen board, and everybody reads the board. If the board says nothing's changed, that's a perfect errand — it cost nothing. And if the store's door is shut, you don't keep rattling it.

## NAYA NOTE

Cold successor: the scarce meters are (1) **GitHub Actions minutes** — ~2,500/month on Shawn's account; every PR push burns CI minutes (macOS runners 10x, Windows 2x), and when minutes run out CI stops and work stops; (2) **GitHub REST API quota** — 5,000/hour for a personal token, zero cost for git protocol reads; (3) **Muse tokens** — paid tokens burn fast, so idle ticks must be near-free. There is NO generic "~2,500 actions/month ≈ 83/day" meter — an older version of this note claimed one; it was wrong and is struck. Operationalize the discipline this way: (1) exactly one scheduled reader (the director pass) touches the GitHub API on a fixed cadence and writes `~/workspace/goals/bring-naya-to-life/hidden_files/shared-state.json`; (2) every other worker's first step is reading shared-state.json and comparing against its watermark — no change = run complete, report nothing; (3) on ANY GitHub 403, set `stand_down=true` with reason and a one-hour `stand_down_until_utc`, then exit immediately — never retry, never probe; (4) distinguish permanent endpoint blocks (e.g., the #1354 comment cap) from rate limits: record the former as state (`issue_1354_comments_disabled`), stand down only for the latter; (5) prefer git protocol for all repo state (tips, trees, files, PR heads) — REST only for comments, check runs, merges, PR metadata; (6) never trigger CI pointlessly — every push is money. Every worker body carries this budget law verbatim.
